# luminous_ui — Project Docs & Continuation System

This `docs/` tree is the **durable memory of the project**. It exists so any new
Claude Code session (or human) can resume work **without reloading the whole
codebase into context**. Read this file first, then load only the docs relevant
to your task.

> **These docs are a guide, not a rulebook.** They capture the current best plan
> and the *reasoning* behind it — not a fixed process to execute blindly. If,
> while working, the code or new context reveals a better or simpler approach,
> **propose it**: say what you'd change and why, and (once it's the direction)
> update the affected doc + record the shift in `decisions.md`. The plans exist
> to be improved, not obeyed. What must be preserved is the *rationale* and the
> *update trail*, so the next session understands why things are the way they are.

## New session? Resume protocol

1. Read **`progress.md`** — the single source of truth for *what's done, what's
   in flight, and where to pick up* (the **Resume point**).
2. Skim **`roadmap.md`** for the big picture (the five phases).
3. Open only the **`workstreams/<area>.md`** you're working on, plus any
   **`reference/`** file it points to. Do **not** read the other workstreams.
4. Follow **`conventions.md`** — especially the sub-agent policy and the
   end-of-session doc-update ritual.

## File map

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `progress.md` | Living status + session log + the current **resume point**. Update every session. |
| `roadmap.md` | The phased plan (P1→P5) and dependencies. |
| `decisions.md` | Decision log (why we chose what) + locked assumptions. |
| `conventions.md` | How we work: sub-agents, doc ritual, code/test/commit rules. |
| `workstreams/backend-data.md` | **P1** — Bun+Hono API, tcgdex→D1 ingest, R2 images, auth, deck API, lobby DO. Contains the tcgdex API reference. |
| `workstreams/deck-builder.md` | **P2** — real cards in the builder, richer filters, editor + decks list. |
| `workstreams/simulator.md` | **P3** — the rules-driven game engine. |
| `workstreams/online.md` | **P4** — run the simulator over the lobby DO for real matches. |
| `workstreams/polish.md` | **P5** — profiles, avatars, lobby names, misc refinement. |
| `reference/ptcg-rules.md` | Condensed Pokémon TCG ruleset — the spec for the simulator (P3). |

## The one rule that keeps this working

**Keep context small.** Delegate research, code-mapping, and multi-file edits to
sub-agents (see `conventions.md`), load only the workstream you need, and write
what you learned back into these docs **before the session ends**.

# Roadmap

Five phases. Each has a detailed workstream doc; this is the map + dependencies.
Live status lives in `progress.md`, not here.

## Phase 1 — Backend & Data Foundation → `workstreams/backend-data.md`
Stand up the Bun + Hono API on Cloudflare. Ingest real tcgdex card data into D1,
mirror images to R2, add accounts + auth (email/password + Discord/Google),
persist decks/folders, and stand up the lobby Durable Object (WebSocket) server.
**Unblocks everything else.**

## Phase 2 — Deck Builder & Decks List (real cards) → `workstreams/deck-builder.md`
Replace the fixture card pool with the live catalog API. Complete the deck
editor (add/remove, counts, format validation, save/load) and the decks list
page (folders, CRUD, persistence). Upgrade filters using the richer tcgdex
fields (set/serie, rarity, HP, illustrator, regulation mark, ability/attack text,
energy cost).
*Depends on: P1 catalog + deck API.*

## Phase 3 — Simulator Engine → `workstreams/simulator.md`
Research the official Pokémon TCG rules (`reference/ptcg-rules.md`) and build the
game engine: a deterministic state machine + a card-effect system driven by the
imported card data + descriptions. Iterative — accuracy improves pass over pass;
unimplemented cards degrade gracefully. The goal is to replicate the real game.
*Depends on: P2 (real, usable decks) + the ruleset.*

## Phase 4 — Online Matches → `workstreams/online.md`
Run the P3 engine authoritatively inside the lobby Durable Object so two players
on different machines can play a real game. Swap the client lobby transport from
BroadcastChannel to WebSocket. Same engine as local play, with tweaks for
authority/hidden info.
*Depends on: P3 engine + P1 lobby DO.*

## Phase 5 — Polish → `workstreams/polish.md`
Now that user + card data exist: player names & profile pictures on the lobby,
profiles, real deck-cover art, and general refinement. Threads through P2–P4 but
tracked separately so it isn't forgotten.
*Depends on: P1 user data.*

1	# Working Conventions
2	
3	## Guidance, not gospel
4	These docs are a **living guide**, not a fixed process. You have context the
5	planning sessions didn't — the actual code, real data, what just broke. Use it:
6	- **Suggest better/different approaches** when you see them. Don't follow a task
7	  list off a cliff because it's written down.
8	- When you deviate: **explain the what + why**, prefer aligning with the user on
9	  anything significant, then **update the affected doc** and log the change in
10	  `decisions.md` (with its rationale). Small in-the-flow improvements don't need
11	  ceremony — just keep the docs honest.
12	- Locked assumptions and D-numbered decisions are **defaults with reasons**, not
13	  laws. Revisit any of them freely; the only hard rule is *don't reverse one
14	  silently* — leave a trail.
15	- Treat file/symbol references in these docs as **point-in-time** — verify against
16	  the current code before relying on them.
17	
18	## Context hygiene (the point of this whole system)
19	- Load **`progress.md` + the one relevant `workstreams/*.md`** (+ its
20	  `reference/`). Don't read unrelated workstreams or sweep the repo.
21	- Prefer facts already written in these docs over re-deriving them.
22	
23	## Sub-agent / workflow policy
24	Delegate to sub-agents to keep the main session's context lean:
25	- **Research** (rules, library docs, API behaviour) → a `general-purpose` agent
26	  that writes a condensed doc into `reference/` and returns only a summary.
27	- **Code mapping** ("how does X work today, what's missing") → an **Explore**
28	  agent (read-only; returns conclusions, not file dumps).
29	- **Implementation** of a self-contained slice → a `general-purpose` agent with
30	  a tight spec; it edits files and returns a summary + what to verify.
31	- **Review** before committing non-trivial work → `/code-review`.
32	- **Big fan-out** (e.g. authoring effect handlers for many cards, or a broad
33	  audit) → a **Workflow** (multi-agent). Note: user-triggered/opt-in — ask first.
34	
35	Rule of thumb: if answering would mean reading many files, delegate it and keep
36	only the conclusion.
37	
38	## Code & quality
39	- TypeScript strict; match the surrounding code's style and comment density.
40	- **Biome** for lint/format; **Vitest** for tests. Run **`bun run check`**
41	  (tsc + biome lint + vitest) before calling work done.
42	- Pure logic gets unit tests (see the many `*.test.ts` in the repo); DOM tests
43	  opt into jsdom per-file (`// @vitest-environment jsdom`).
44	
45	## Git / commits
46	- Branch off `main` for non-trivial work; commit/push only when asked.
47	- Commit trailer per global config: `Co-Authored-By: Claude ...`.
48	
49	## End-of-session ritual (do not skip)
50	1. Update `progress.md`: status table + session-log entry + **new resume point**.
51	2. Record any decision in `decisions.md`.
52	3. Write anything learned into the right workstream/reference doc so the next
53	   session doesn't rediscover it.
54

# Working Conventions

## Guidance, not gospel
These docs are a **living guide**, not a fixed process. You have context the
planning sessions didn't — the actual code, real data, what just broke. Use it:
- **Suggest better/different approaches** when you see them. Don't follow a task
  list off a cliff because it's written down.
- When you deviate: **explain the what + why**, prefer aligning with the user on
  anything significant, then **update the affected doc** and log the change in
  `decisions.md` (with its rationale). Small in-the-flow improvements don't need
  ceremony — just keep the docs honest.
- Locked assumptions and D-numbered decisions are **defaults with reasons**, not
  laws. Revisit any of them freely; the only hard rule is *don't reverse one
  silently* — leave a trail.
- Treat file/symbol references in these docs as **point-in-time** — verify against
  the current code before relying on them.

## Context hygiene (the point of this whole system)
- Load **`progress.md` + the one relevant `workstreams/*.md`** (+ its
  `reference/`). Don't read unrelated workstreams or sweep the repo.
- Prefer facts already written in these docs over re-deriving them.

## Sub-agent / workflow policy
Delegate to sub-agents to keep the main session's context lean:
- **Research** (rules, library docs, API behaviour) → a `general-purpose` agent
  that writes a condensed doc into `reference/` and returns only a summary.
- **Code mapping** ("how does X work today, what's missing") → an **Explore**
  agent (read-only; returns conclusions, not file dumps).
- **Implementation** of a self-contained slice → a `general-purpose` agent with
  a tight spec; it edits files and returns a summary + what to verify.
- **Review** before committing non-trivial work → `/code-review`.

  audit) → a **Workflow** (multi-agent). Note: user-triggered/opt-in — ask first.

content.content: 127:| D86 | A deck cover is a PIN over the derived default, resolved on read (P5 polish, increment P5-6) | P5-3 fronted every deck with its highest-HP Pokémon and said outright that the proper answer was letting the owner choose. This is that: a nullable `decks.cover_card_id` the editor sets, and a pure **`effectiveCoverCardId(chosen, candidates)`** the list query runs — **the pin wins, and everything else falls through to `pickCoverCardId`**. The derived rule is untouched; it is now explicitly the DEFAULT rather than the answer. **Three decisions carry the slice.** First, **the resolution runs against the candidate list the default was already deriving from**, so honouring a choice costs NO extra query, and a pin that has gone stale (its card removed elsewhere, or its scan gone after a re-ingest) silently falls back instead of drawing a blank rectangle — a deck must never front a card it doesn't run. Second, **the pin may be a TRAINER or an Energy while the derived default stays Pokémon-only**: guessing needs a rule, choosing does not, and a signature Supporter is a legitimate face (browser-verified with Academy at Night, which the rule could never pick). Third, **two fields, deliberately not one**: `DeckSummary.coverCardId` remains the face being DRAWN (so the grid needed no change at all), while the full `Deck` carries `chosenCoverCardId`, the stored CHOICE the editor's picker is set to — null for almost every deck. Collapsing them into one name would have made "what is drawn" and "what was chosen" the same word for two different questions. **`Automatic` is an explicit option in the picker**, not the absence of one, so reverting is one click; it deliberately shows no art, because the default is a RULE and drawing today's answer to it would read as "this card". **The consistency rule lives on both sides:** PATCH validates the pin against the card list the patch LEAVES BEHIND (400 `cover card not in deck`) and drops a pin whose card that patch removes, while the editor's `toSnapshot` drops it locally too — not cosmetic, since the cover rides the same debounced PATCH as the card list, and a self-contradicting body would 400 forever (the saver retries the same dirty snapshot). The cover joining that one save path is what keeps the pair atomic. 1911 → **1932** tests; migration `0004`. **BROWSER-VERIFIED end to end at 1920×1080:** pinning the Trainer put it on the library tile, removing it dropped the pin, kept saving ("Saved", PATCH 200 — the wedge that would have followed a naive implementation) and fell back to Absol; a pin survived a reload through GET /decks/:id; a hand-crafted PATCH naming a card outside the deck got the 400; and both the footer control and a picker tile hit-tested to themselves. *Why: a heuristic that is right most of the time plus an override that is always right beats trying to make the heuristic cleverer — and the override is only trustworthy if the two can never disagree about what the deck contains.* (2026-07-26) |

1	// User-data tables (read-write): accounts, auth and deck persistence.
2	// Spec: docs/workstreams/backend-data.md §5.3 (schema) + §3.5 (auth model).
3	//
4	// Timestamps here are INTEGER epoch milliseconds (`mode: "timestamp_ms"`,
5	// surfaced as Date by drizzle) — unlike the catalog, these are OUR clocks, so
6	// nothing forces ISO text on us, and integers give unambiguous SQL comparison
7	// (`expires_at < ?now` for session sweeps) with no string-format drift.
8	// `created_at`-style columns default to `unixepoch() * 1000` in the DB so a
9	// forgotten insert value can never produce a row without a timestamp.
10	
11	import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
12	import { foreignKey, index, integer, primaryKey, sqliteTable, text } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";
13	import { cards } from "./catalog";
14	
15	/** DB-side default for epoch-ms timestamp columns. */
16	const nowMs = sql`(unixepoch() * 1000)`;
17	
18	export const users = sqliteTable("users", {
19	  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
20	  email: text("email").notNull().unique(),
21	  displayName: text("display_name").notNull(),
22	  /** Null for OAuth-only accounts (§3.5: password and OAuth can coexist). */
23	  passwordHash: text("password_hash"),
24	  emailVerified: integer("email_verified", { mode: "boolean" }).notNull().default(false),
25	  createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" }).notNull().default(nowMs),
26	});

1	// The deck-library Deck (P1 milestone 7 — backend-data.md §5.2/§6): the web
2	// app's existing `Deck` vocabulary (src/features/decks/data.ts) extended with
3	// the persisted card list. Two projections:
4	//   - `Deck` — the full resource (GET /decks/:id): carries `cards`.
5	//   - `DeckSummary` — the list row (GET /decks): `cards` replaced by
6	//     `cardCount`, the summed counts, which is exactly the web shape's field.
7	
8	import { z } from "zod";
9	
10	/** One deck entry: a catalog card id ("sv01-001") and how many copies.
11	    Counts are 1–99 — 0 means "remove the entry", and 99 is a sanity cap
12	    (real formats allow 4, but the builder must not enforce format legality
13	    at the persistence layer). */
14	export const deckCardSchema = z.object({
15	  cardId: z.string().min(1),
16	  count: z.number().int().min(1).max(99),
17	});
18	export type DeckCard = z.infer<typeof deckCardSchema>;
19	
20	/** Everything but the card list — shared by `Deck` and `DeckSummary`. */
21	const deckBaseSchema = z.object({
22	  id: z.string(),
23	  name: z.string(),
24	  /** Play format ("standard" | "expanded" | …) — free text mirroring the
25	      nullable DB column; null when the player hasn't picked one. */
26	  format: z.string().nullable(),
27	  /** Base hue (0–360) for the deck's cover gradient (web `Deck.tint`). */
28	  tint: z.number().int().min(0).max(360),
29	  /** Owning folder, or null when the deck lives at the library root. */
30	  folderId: z.string().nullable(),
31	  /** Manual sort slot within the library — lists come back ordered by it
32	      ascending. Global per user (not per folder): a nest move keeps the
33	      deck's slot, exactly like the web grid's flat array. New decks take
34	      min-1 (they prepend), so negatives are normal. */
35	  position: z.number().int(),
36	  /** ISO datetime — the api serializes the epoch-ms DB column at the boundary. */
37	  updated: z.iso.datetime(),
38	});
39	
40	/** The full deck resource — what GET /decks/:id (and create/patch) serve. */
41	export const deckSchema = deckBaseSchema.extend({
42	  cards: z.array(deckCardSchema),
43	  /** The cover the OWNER picked (P5-6), or null for "automatic" — the default
44	      the server derives from the contents. Deliberately NOT the same field as
45	      `DeckSummary.coverCardId`, which is the face actually being drawn: this is
46	      the stored CHOICE, the editor's state, and it is null for almost every
47	      deck. PATCH /decks/:id takes it under the same name. */
48	  chosenCoverCardId: z.string().nullable(),
49	});
50	export type Deck = z.infer<typeof deckSchema>;
51	
52	/** The GET /decks list row: no card list, just the summed copy count. */
53	export const deckSummarySchema = deckBaseSchema.extend({
54	  cardCount: z.number().int().min(0),
55	  /** The card whose art fronts this deck in the library grid — the owner's
56	      `chosenCoverCardId` when they picked one that is still in the deck and
57	      drawable (P5-6), else the derived default (P5-3, `pickCoverCardId`), else
58	      null for a deck with nothing to show (an empty one, or one whose Pokémon
59	      have no scan yet). Resolved server-side on read, so it follows the deck's
60	      contents with nothing to keep in sync. */
61	  coverCardId: z.string().nullable(),
62	});
63	export type DeckSummary = z.infer<typeof deckSummarySchema>;

8	export const userSchema = z.object({
9	  id: z.string(),
10	  email: z.email(),
11	  displayName: z.string(),
12	  emailVerified: z.boolean(),
13	  /** The account's generated-avatar token (P5-2), derived server-side from the
14	      id — the SAME value a lobby seat carries in `PlayerState.avatarSeed`, so
15	      the face a player sees on their own profile is the face opponents see.

17	  avatarSeed: z.string(),
18	  /** ISO datetime — the api serializes the epoch-ms DB column at the boundary. */
19	  createdAt: z.iso.datetime(),
20	});
21	export type User = z.infer<typeof userSchema>;

### Prior header (P4 3c-viii — half-open socket liveness, kept for continuity)
**Last updated (was):** 2026-07-26 — build session #63 (**P4 3c-viii — half-open socket liveness**). The gap
3c-v's browser run surfaced, and the last known way an online match could stall. `setWebSocketAutoResponse`
answers the client's 1.5s ping WITHOUT waking the DO — the thing that makes hibernation worth having — but it
also means the DO can never notice pings that **stop**. A network that dies without a TCP close therefore
left a socket that looked perfectly live forever: `hasSocket` said yes, no disconnect grace was armed, no
forfeit clock started, and the opponent waited indefinitely. Every ORDINARY exit (tab close, browser kill,
navigation, reload, crash) delivers a close event, which is why this never bit in practice and why it took a
deliberate `set offline` to reproduce. **The fix reads the signal the runtime was already recording:**
`state.getWebSocketAutoResponseTimestamp(ws)` returns when it last auto-answered that socket, so liveness
costs nothing at ping time. The alternative — dropping the auto-response and stamping `lastSeen` in
`webSocketMessage` — was rejected on exactly that ground: ~40 wakes a minute per socket, hibernation given
up, to learn what the runtime already knows. **What it costs instead is a POLL,** because a quiet in-game
lobby schedules no alarm at all: `scheduleMaintenance` now pushes a **`LIVENESS_SWEEP_MS`** (30s) deadline
whenever any socket is connected, so an occupied lobby wakes twice a minute. **`SOCKET_SILENCE_MS`** is 15s —
ten missed pings, so a phone changing networks or a throttled background tab is not mistaken for a dead one —
and a test pins the budget that matters: sweep + silence + the 5s grace all fit inside the 90s forfeit, so a
dead network can never resolve SLOWER than a closed tab. A `null` timestamp counts as **ALIVE**, deliberately:
it is the state of every connection before its first ping, and nothing can distinguish "just opened" from
"opened long ago and never pinged". **The sweep only CLOSES** — the grace, the seat going disconnected and
the forfeit are all machinery a real close already drives, reached through the same `socketGone` (called
explicitly, since a server-side `close()` delivers no `webSocketClose` event to us). engine RULES UNCHANGED
(0.41.0); 1874 → **1878** tests. `bun run check` green. Built solo with full context; **self-reviewed, no
independent reviewer this session**. **BROWSER-VERIFIED with the very reproducer that exposed the bug:** with
a match live, one client was put offline with its socket left OPEN — before this change that produced nothing
at all, and now the opponent saw "disconnected — forfeits in 1:30" after ~50s (15s silence + up to 30s sweep
+ the 5s grace) with the countdown running. Bringing the client back online restored it within ~10s (the
channel reconnected, re-helloed, the forfeit was cancelled), while the client that stayed connected
throughout was never swept. Zero page errors. **With this, P4 has no known defects and no planned work left.**

that wedges if the answer never comes. A plain `endMatch` dropping both players on the versus screen to

mechanism: the countdown still starts only when BOTH seats are ready, so pressing Rematch *is* the offer,
readying *is* the acceptance, and un-readying on the versus screen *is* the withdrawal — all through
machinery that already exists and is already tested, with **no new lobby state at all**. The pure helper is
literally `applyIntent(endMatch(snapshot), slot, {type:"set-ready", ready:true})`; going through
`applyIntent` rather than writing `ready: true` keeps "you can't be ready without a deck" in ONE place, so a
player whose saved deck vanished between games lands back un-readied instead of in an impossible state.

property of the snapshot the shared reducer sees: only the DO can tell whether the match it holds has
actually reached `gameOver`, and a rematch during a LIVE game must be refused (conceding is how you leave one

a stale record on the way past; `commit` then sees the lobby leave in-game, `abandonsMatch` fires and
`MATCH_KEY` is dropped — which is exactly what makes the next handoff mint a FRESH game instead of hitting

argument defaulting to null (so you cannot write one without deciding the other), and

normalizer that fills fields added since the write — deliberately the OPPOSITE of D72's `MatchRecord` answer,

one sensible value, and being wrong is cosmetic), and the guard is on the field's TYPE, not on nullishness,

the projection (`koParkActiveSeat` gained `attackEpilogue` as an in-turn marker).

**Board conditions are live (P3-M5, D40) — one `BoardCondition` vocabulary, TWO
consumers.** The `conditionalPlay` family, built as a primitive instead of a per-card
flag. **`BoardCondition`** (effects.ts) is a predicate union evaluated for ONE seat —
**`morePrizesThanOpponent`** (strict `>`: you are BEHIND on Prizes taken),
**`yourStadiumInPlay`**, **`noEnergyOnYourPokemon`** (Active AND Bench, Basic or
Special) — behind a single evaluator **`conditionHolds`** and a printed-text describer

state**, which is exactly why **a gate emits no event** — contrast `coinFlipGate`,
whose flip is genuinely new information; a board condition is a fact both players can
read off the table, and the branch's own ops emit whatever happened.

would-only-whiff heuristics: this is a rule PRINTED on the card. Named `trainer…`

precedent; it is also why Luxray's Ability gate must NOT be authored here).

### Prior resume point (P3-M5 Iono, kept for continuity)
**Iono is live (P3-M5, D39) — the hand-refresh Supporter family is CLOSED.** The
format's highest-play-rate Supporter needed **no new op**: three composable riders on
the D38 `handRefresh` op. **`toBottom?: true`** — the PLACEMENT: shuffle the **hand
alone** and append it UNDER the deck (`[...deck, ...shuffle(hand)]`) instead of
shuffling it into the deck, so the deck's existing order — and therefore the very next
draws — SURVIVE (the whole strategic point of Iono over Judge; pinned by a test
asserting the drawn cards are EXACTLY the pre-play deck top, in order).
**`draw:{kind:"prizeCount"}`** — each affected player draws their OWN remaining Prize
count (the player behind draws more); a Prize count is public, so the draw size leaks
nothing. **`onlyIfAnyMoved?: true`** — the draw clause fires only if ≥1 affected player
actually moved ≥1 card: an **all-or-nothing gate ACROSS the seats** ("if EITHER
player…"), not per-seat. That gate forced the op's one structural change: **two passes**
over the affected seats (all placements, then all draws) instead of D38's interleaved
move-then-draw — **behaviour-preserving** for Youngster/Judge/Brassius/Katy (per-seat
disjoint zones + `drawToHand` consumes NO rng ⇒ byte-identical states and rng threading,
verified by reconstructing the old loop and diffing at 3 seeds each); the only change is
Judge's event INTERLEAVING (SHUFFLED p1, SHUFFLED p2, DRAWN p1, DRAWN p2 — which also
reads truer to the printed sentence). `shuffle` consumes nothing for a length ≤ 1 input,
so an Iono into two empty hands advances the rng ZERO times. One new count-only event
**`HAND_TO_BOTTOM_OF_DECK {seat, count}`** — distinct from its sibling because the public
fact differs (the deck's order is untouched, which both players must be able to read off
the log). **Web: one log row, no dialog** (never parks, no projection change) — "shuffled
their hand (N cards) and put it on the bottom of their deck": it must say BOTH verbs,
since the hand IS randomized on its way under an unshuffled deck. Lands **Iono**

first, then — for `both` — the opponent) it captures the PRE-shuffle hand size, moves

| D87 | A favourite deck is a validated PIN of the account's OWN deck, resolved on read (P5 polish, increment P5-7) | Joins P5-5 (an editable profile) and P5-6 (a deck's cover art): an account pins one of its own decks as its favourite and sees that deck's cover + name on /settings. A nullable **`users.favourite_deck_id`** (migration `0005`) surfaced as **`userSchema.favouriteDeckId`** — **just the ID.** **Three choices.** First, **store only the id, not the deck's name/cover:** /settings resolves those from the caller's own `GET /decks` list, so a rename or re-cover shows through with no stale copy and a favourite whose deck has vanished resolves to a blank tile — the SAME "derive on read, tolerate stale" the covers use (D83/D86). Second, **a favourite must be one of YOUR decks:** `PATCH /auth/me` gains an OPTIONAL nullable `favouriteDeckId` (absent leaves it, null clears it, a string is validated against the caller's decks) and 400s `favourite deck not found` for anyone else's id or a phantom — the account can never point at a deck it doesn't own, mirroring D86's `cover card not in deck`. The users↔decks mutual reference forced an `AnySQLiteColumn` annotation to break the TS type cycle. The picker is a native `<select>` in the SAME form as the name, riding ONE PATCH so name + favourite save atomically; the provider adopts the answer, so the corner control follows with no re-probe. 1932 → **1936** tests. NOT browser-verified this session (budget) — covered by a new DOM round-trip test + schema units; flagged for browser verification next session. *Why: the profile only needs to REFERENCE a deck, and the deck already owns its name and cover — copying them onto the account would just be a second source of truth to keep in sync; the id plus resolve-on-read is the whole feature, and the validated pin + SET NULL make "your favourite is always a real deck of yours" true by construction.* (2026-07-27) |

## Product / architecture decisions
| # | Decision | Choice |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Backend data strategy | Own DB — ingest tcgdex → Cloudflare D1, serve our own API |
| D2 | Accounts & persistence | Full accounts + auth; users own their decks |
| D2a | Auth methods | Email + password **and** social OAuth (Discord + Google) |

| D7 | Game engine placement | Separate **`packages/engine`** (pure logic) — imported by both `apps/web` (local play) and `apps/api` (authoritative DO). *Why: the engine runs in two runtimes; an app can't import another app.* |
| D8 | Card-effect modeling | **Composable, data-driven op programs** over shared archetype templates (not per-card functions); engine emits **semantic events** consumed by the animation layer. *Why: cards are minor variations on a few archetypes; keeps authoring + animation cheap. Detail in `workstreams/simulator.md`.* |
| D9 | Image mirroring & ingest execution (refines D4/§3.4) | Images mirror into R2 **lazily** — a Worker route (`GET /assets/…`) serves from R2 and on miss fetches tcgdex origin, stores, streams; catalog rows keep tcgdex **origin** URLs. Card-data backfill runs as a **local Bun script** applying batched upsert SQL via `wrangler d1 execute`; a future cron does small in-Worker deltas only. *Why: a full SV backfill is ~10k images — over Worker subrequest limits in one shot and hours of CLI puts; cache-aside mirrors exactly what's viewed and stays within limits.* (2026-07-09) |
| D10 | M9 catalog search shape (refines D5/§6) | `CardBrief` **extended** with `types/hp/regulationMark/stage/trainerType/energyType` (card-table columns only — **no set join**, so no `setName`); `GET /cards` gains **repeatable `type`/`rarity`** (OR within a dimension) and **`sort=name\|hp-desc\|set`**; KV cache keys version-prefixed (`catalog:v2:`) so a shape change can't serve stale briefs. The builder consumes briefs through one adapter (`src/features/builder/catalog.ts` — accented `"Pokémon"`, stage/trainerType/energyType → the single `subtype`). *Why: the grid/filters/deck-math need those fields per tile; per-tile full-Card fetches or a fixture pool were the alternatives.* (2026-07-13) |
| D11 | M9 scope trims (pending P2) | **Kinds** (`subtypes`) filter stays a client-side per-page heuristic (server can't express OR across stage/trainerType; EX/Mega are name-regexes until structured data — P2 tasks 8-9). **Manual deck/folder reorder is session-only** (no position field in the schema — P2 task 17). **Folder delete keeps the lift-up UX client-side** (child PATCHes before DELETE) over the server's cascade semantics. **`RARITIES` is a hardcoded tcgdex vocabulary snapshot** in the rail. *Why: each would widen M9's already-large surface; all four are logged with their fixes in `workstreams/deck-builder.md`.* (2026-07-13) **Revised 2026-07-14 (P2-M1):** kinds now filter **server-side** (repeatable `stage`/`trainerType`/`energyType`) — only EX/Mega remain a client-side name-regex post-filter (tcgdex `suffix` not persisted; follow-up logged); hardcoded vocabularies replaced by **`GET /facets`**. Reorder (task 17) and lift-up remain as decided. **Revised again 2026-07-14 (task 17):** reorder is now persisted — see D13; only the lift-up trim still stands. |
| D12 | P2-M1 catalog surface & legality source of truth | `GET /cards` gains **repeatable `id`** (≤100, deck hydration in ONE call; chunked IN + in-memory ordering twin of the SQL sort), **`nameExact`** (case-insensitive whole-name equality), `serie`, `illustrator`, `text` (LIKE over ability/attack JSON), plus the kind params above; **`GET /facets`** serves the filter vocabularies (7 DISTINCTs, one db.batch, KV-cached). `CardBrief` += **`legal {standard,expanded}`**; KV namespace → **`catalog:v3:`**, with KV **bypassed** for >512-byte keys and any `?id=` request (per-deck id sets never recur — caching them is pure write waste). Web: **`Format.legalFlag`** keys BOTH the `legalOnly` filter (`legal=<flag>`) and `isLegalInFormat` (structured verdict beats printed mark; mark check only for legal-less fixtures) — one legality definition for grid + validator. Deck rules: **Radiant = 1 per deck total** (like ACE SPEC; official rule), Prism Star = 1 per name. *Why: filters needed server truth for correct totals; hydration was an N-request fan-out; legality had two disagreeing definitions.* (2026-07-14) |
| D13 | Manual-order persistence model (P2 task 17) | `position` INTEGER on `decks` and `folders` — **global per user, not per folder**: the web grid's flat array (position-ascending) IS the manual order, per-view filtering preserves relative order, and a nest move keeps the row's slot (folderId changes, position doesn't) — exactly the client's existing semantics. Creates take **min−1** (new rows prepend); migration 0003 backfills existing rows in the old name-order so nothing visibly moves. A reorder permutes the in-view rows **among their own slots' position values** (`applyReorder` returns the rewritten array + the changed `{id, position}` pairs) and persists via **`POST /decks/reorder` / `/folders/reorder`** — absolute assignments, ≤500 rows, applied atomically in one db.batch; unknown/foreign ids → 400 naming them; failure recovery is **resync**, not per-row rollback (the folder-delete precedent). | D14 | Engine core contract (P3-M1) | **`applyAction(state, action) → {ok:true, state, events} | {ok:false, error}`** — one reducer, never throws, never mutates. `GameState` is plain JSON (the mulberry32 `rngState` lives **inside** it, so same seed + same actions replay identically); card instances are **uids** (`"p1#0"`) over an injected `cardPool` carried in the state (keeps `applyAction` a pure 2-arg pair and snapshots self-contained). Seats **`p1`/`p2` are labels, not turn order** — the coin winner *chooses* first via an action, `firstPlayer` records it. **Choices are actions; mandatory steps auto-resolve** inside the reducer (mulligan redraws, prize setting, the turn-start draw), so a `Phase` exists only where a player owes a decision. **Events are the animation + wire contract** (semantic, serializable, payloads always copied — never aliasing state or the caller's action). **Wire-safety:** TS types are not input validation — P4 decodes actions from clients, so every index/seat/count an action carries is runtime-checked (three real card-destroying bugs came from exactly this: a JSON string `"1"` bench index). *Why: the engine runs in two runtimes (web local play + the authoritative DO), and an authoritative server needs a total, replayable, non-throwing function of (state, action).* (2026-07-14) |
| D15 | Mulligan compensation (rules correction) | Each player may draw 1 card **per opponent mulligan**, and **mulliganing yourself does not forfeit it** — so **both** seats can be owed at once (each off the other's count). `reference/ptcg-rules.md` §3.5 previously read "the non-mulliganing player", which the M1 engine implemented as an exemption that does not exist; the reference doc is corrected and the phase now carries a per-seat `owed`/`decided` map. The compensation draw is **clamped** so a player can never draw below the 6 cards they must still set aside as prizes. *Why: a wrong rule in the spec propagated straight into the engine — the reference doc is the source of truth and had to be fixed at the source.* (2026-07-14) |
| D16 | M2 staged turn tail, KO interrupts & damage modifiers (P3-M2) | The turn tail is a **`pending: PendingStage[]` queue** on `GameState`, drained by `advance()` (flow.ts): automatic stages run, decision stages either **park** (phase becomes the matching `ko:takePrizes`/`ko:promote` interrupt, prompt event emitted) or **auto-resolve** when only one legal resolution exists. `attack` seeds `takePrizes`+`promote` ahead of the shared `turnTail(seat)` triple. The parked phase mirrors `pending[0]` (dual encoding, kept deliberately for M2): handlers cross-check the two and reject with **`PHASE_DESYNC`** on mismatch. Win evaluation lives in ONE place — the shared `resolvePrizesAndResume`/`resolvePromotionAndResume` helpers used by both the action handlers and advance's auto-resolves. `gameOver` carries **`GameOutcome`** (`win {winner, reason}` \| `tie {reasons}`); sudden death is surfaced as `tie`, not played out. Printed weakness/resistance parse to a **`DamageModifier {op: multiply\|add\|subtract, amount}`** (×N / +N / −N; unknown garble keeps modern-era ×2/−30 defaults) applied weakness→resistance, floor 0 (§8.5); `DAMAGE_DEALT` carries the modifiers so animators can show the math. Data gaps never guess a KO: `hp ≤ 0` reads as the null data gap. *Why: KO resolution must pause mid-tail for player choices, M3's checkup KOs reuse the same interrupts, and additive legacy weakness ("+20", schema-documented) was being silently misread as ×2.* (2026-07-16) |
| D17 | Engine→playmat projection contract (P3) | **`projectGameState(state, viewerSeat) → GameProjection`** (`src/features/game/projection.ts`): `{ board, piles, pokemon, turn, activePlayer, waitingOn, pendingDecision, outcome }` — `board` is a drop-in playmat `BoardState` (`you` = viewer); the wrapper carries what BoardState can't (`piles` deckCount/discard, `pokemon` = per-uid `{damage, hp}`, `outcome` per-viewer win/tie). **`activePlayer` = turn owner; `waitingOn` = the seat that must act NOW** — the split exists because during `ko:promote` the actor is the NON-turn player (the KO'd defender), and a UI gating on turn ownership alone soft-locks. Hidden info is redacted structurally: opponent hand = positional backs (`opponent-hand-N`, no uids — a uid is stable across zones and would let a client track a hidden card), both prize piles = counts only, decks = counts. Public cards key off the engine **uid** so the Pixi layer animates a card as one object across projections. The phase mapping is an **exhaustive switch** (`satisfies never`) — a new engine phase is a compile error, not a silent guess. *Why: this is the same per-viewer filter P4's server will apply; building it client-side first pins the contract with tests.* (2026-07-16) **Revised 2026-07-17 (wire-up review):** during any `setup:*` phase the OPPONENT's active/bench also project as face-down backs (positional `-hidden` ids, no `pokemon` rows — a row would leak the uid key + printed HP); a hot-seat viewer flip at Ready was exposing the first player's face-down placements. Reveal re-keys positional→uid (remount, not flip) — the same trade as hand backs. |

| D18 | Local play page & engine card-pool sourcing (P3 wire-up) | **`/play`** is a hot-seat local match: `GamePage` owns `GameState` via `useLocalGame` (pure reducer over `applyAction`), renders `projectGameState` through the extracted presentational **`PlaymatView`** (the `/simulator` mock, retitled "Sandbox", is a thin wrapper driver), and the **viewer follows `waitingOn`** for the device flip. The engine `cardPool` is built client-side by **fanning out `GET /cards/:id`** (`src/features/game/cardPool.ts`, concurrency 8, module-level promise cache; 404s cache as stable `missing`, rejections self-evict) — NOT via the brief-returning batch route. *Why: `CardBrief` deliberately omits the combat blobs (attacks/weakness/retreat) the engine reads; the per-id route already serves the full canonical Card KV-cached, and this needed no api change while api deploys stay user-gated. A `?full` batch param is the logged follow-up to bundle with the next deploy.* (2026-07-17) |
| D19 | Drop-legality is a driver-supplied predicate (P3 wire-up review) | `AnimatedCardsLayer` takes an optional **`PlacementPredicate`** (defaults to the sandbox's `canPlace`, so the mock is untouched); `/play` supplies `gamePlacementPredicate(game, viewerSeat)` — a deliberately **coarse, gesture-class** gate (phase-aware: what CAN ever map to an action) kept in lockstep with `moveToAction` by a property test (every afforded drop translates to a non-null action). Fine-grained legality stays with `applyAction` + the error pill. Hand→hand reorder is rejected on /play (the engine owns hand order; affording it was a silent lie). *Why: the phase-unaware mock `canPlace` afforded gestures the engine could never accept (accept-animation → wrong-rule error pill), and M4 evolve/trainer drags can't be expressed through it — the seam had to move to the driver.* (2026-07-17) |
| D20 | Text-derived attack effects (P3-M3) | Status-applying attacks resolve through a **conservative exact-sentence deriver** (`packages/engine/src/effects.ts`): five anchored whole-effect patterns ("Your opponent's Active Pokémon is now {X}.", the coin-flip-gated variant, "This Pokémon is now {X}.", the Rest heal compound, the raised-poison Checkup variant) compile to a tiny **`EffectStep[]`** program (applyStatus/heal/coinFlipGate) executed after damage, before the KO check; ANY other text keeps today's loud `ATTACK_EFFECT_SKIPPED`. | D24 | Persistent-zone Trainers via a continuous-modifier pipeline (P3-M4 slice 3) | Stadiums (§7.3) and Pokémon Tools (§7.4) don't run op **programs** — their effects are **continuous**, so a new module **`packages/engine/src/continuous.ts`** aggregates them and is the ONE place a rule read consults them: `effectiveRetreatCost` (turn.ts retreat), `effectiveAttackCost` (attack.ts cost check), `effectiveMaxHp` (flow.ts `isLethallyDamaged` — the KO test — and the web `battle.hp`), and `passivesOf` (attack.ts damage: a defender's post-W/R reduction — now Bouffalant "Bouffer" **and** a defending Tool — plus an attacker's pre-W/R bonus). **Stadium** is a single shared **`GameState.stadium` {uid, owner}**: `playTrainer` routes Stadiums to `playStadium` (one/turn via a new `stadiumPlayed` allowance; replace-on-play discards the predecessor to **its owner's** pile; the same-**NAME** ban compares names not ids, so the sv02-171/sv03-229 "Artazon" reprints can't self-replace); allowed on turn 1 (§4 bans only Supporters + attacking). **Tool** is a new action **`attachTool`** (NOT playTrainer — it carries a target): one per Pokémon, uncapped per turn, no allowance consumed, no detach — it rides the stack through evolution and discards with a KO'd stack (the `tools` slot M1 reserved is finally populated). (optional W/R clarifier). **Web:** the ONLY source change is `projection.ts koParkActiveSeat` treating `resumeTurn` as in-turn (a mid-turn KO park still reports the actor as `activePlayer`); the exhaustive `phaseViewOf` Phase switch is untouched (`resumeTurn` is a PendingStage, not a Phase), and the log/HUD need nothing — `DAMAGE_DEALT`/`KNOCKED_OUT` resolve a benched uid the same way, and the opponent's mid-turn prize pick rides the existing `waitingOn` viewer-follow. | D27 | Triggered Abilities via event scan points (P3-M4 slice 6) | Triggered Abilities (§9) — the ones that FIRE on a game event, not player-activated — get a **`TriggeredAbility`** entry on `CardProgram.triggered` (`{ name; trigger; program; optional?; activeOnly? }`) run through the shared interpreter by a small **`triggers.ts`** wired at **three scan points**: **`onPlayToBench`** (turn.ts playBasicToBench — a turn play, NOT a setup placement), **`onEvolve`** (turn.ts evolve), **`betweenTurns`** (flow.ts runCheckup). Defaulting the missing fields on read — the fix the LOW originally proposed — was REJECTED: it repairs only the fields we happen to know went missing, and says nothing about the far more dangerous case, an embedded engine `GameState` written by a build whose RULES have since moved, which reads back "fine" and then plays subtly wrong. A version covers both, and it is what makes "no migrations" a loud, recoverable condition instead of a silent hazard. Their safety is structural twice over — every handler that can change the game gates on `attachedPlayer`, which stays null for them, and the board they receive is the one that withholds both hands. `attachPlayer` clears the flag, so a watcher who later takes a freed seat stops getting the seatless board. **Players are NOT told they are being watched** — chosen deliberately: telling them needs a spectator count on the wire and a broadcast on every join/leave, and the lobby already treats a refused socket silently. Recorded here so the next session can reverse it knowingly rather than discover it. **Deliberate consequence:** anyone with (or guessing) a 4-character lobby code can watch a game in progress. What they get is a public table — both boards, no hands, no deck order, no prizes — which is the intended product behaviour, not an oversight. **Client:** `useLobby`'s sticky `rejected` boolean became `refusal: "full" | "kicked" | null`, because the two are no longer the same thing — a KICK is terminal, while "full" keeps the connection, keeps accepting `state` (for the players' names) and `match` (the board), and flips the status to `spectating` on the first board. Its hello retry moved to the idle-driven cadence heartbeats already keep fresh, so a spectator whose socket drops re-announces and is re-marked, without becoming a retry storm against a lobby that is simply full. `OnlineMatch` gained `spectating`, which removes every control (`OnlineHud`, Concede, Rematch, drags, Pass, the forfeit banner), keeps the board, the LOG and the result, and asks a leave question that costs nothing. 1865 → **1874** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED with a third, signed-out profile on the same lobby link:** the board rendered; at `setup:place` the player saw their own hand as "Skeledirge; Skeledirge; Rare Candy; …" while the spectator saw "Face-down card" ×7 for BOTH hands — the hidden-information property, live; the spectator had no Concede/Ready/Rematch and a disabled Pass; a concede propagated to them instantly with the result but no Rematch; a rematch dropped them back to "Lobby is full" (the watch-a-match-not-a-lobby rule); and they picked the NEXT match up automatically when it started. Zero page errors on all three. **The run caught a real bug:** `state` frames only go out on a lobby COMMIT, so a spectator joining mid-match never received one and their board read "Host vs Guest" — `refuseSeat` now sends the snapshot explicitly. *Why: the cheapest correct entry point is one that already exists. "Refused a seat" and "may watch" are the same fact about a socket, so deriving one from the other costs a branch instead of a protocol, and the rule it implies — matches are watchable, lobbies are not — is the one you would have chosen anyway.* (2026-07-26) |

| D80 | Half-open sockets are swept with the runtime's OWN keepalive timestamp (P4 online, increment 3c-viii) | The gap 3c-v's browser run surfaced, and the last known way an online match could stall. `setWebSocketAutoResponse` answers the client's 1.5s ping without waking the DO — the thing that makes hibernation worth having — but it also means the DO can never notice pings that STOP. A network that dies without a TCP close therefore left a socket that looked perfectly live forever: `hasSocket` said yes, no disconnect grace was armed, no forfeit clock started, and the opponent waited indefinitely. Every ORDINARY exit (tab close, browser kill, navigation, reload, crash) delivers a close event, which is why this never bit in practice and why it took a deliberate `set offline` to reproduce. **The fix is to read the signal the runtime was already recording:** `state.getWebSocketAutoResponseTimestamp(ws)` returns when it last auto-answered that socket, so liveness costs nothing at ping time. The alternative — dropping the auto-response and stamping `lastSeen` in `webSocketMessage` — was rejected on exactly that ground: it would wake the DO ~40 times a minute per socket and give up hibernation to learn what the runtime already knows. **What it costs instead is a POLL**, because a quiet in-game lobby schedules no alarm at all: `scheduleMaintenance` now pushes a `LIVENESS_SWEEP_MS` (30s) deadline whenever any socket is connected, so an occupied lobby wakes twice a minute. `SOCKET_SILENCE_MS` is 15s — ten missed pings, so a phone changing networks or a throttled background tab is not mistaken for a dead one — and a test pins the budget that matters: sweep + silence + the 5s grace all fit inside the 90s forfeit, so a dead network can never resolve slower than a closed tab. **A `null` timestamp counts as ALIVE**, deliberately: it is the state of every connection before its first ping, and nothing can distinguish "just opened" from "opened long ago and never pinged" — the cost of that reading is a socket we never sweep, versus closing a healthy one-second-old connection. **The sweep only CLOSES**; everything after it — the grace, the seat going disconnected, the forfeit — is the machinery a real close already drives, reached through the same `socketGone` (called explicitly, since a server-side `close()` delivers no `webSocketClose` event to us). 1874 → **1878** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED with the very reproducer that exposed the bug:** with a match live, one client was put offline with the socket left open; before this change that produced nothing at all, and now the opponent saw "disconnected — forfeits in 1:30" after ~50s (15s silence + up to 30s sweep + the 5s grace) and the countdown ran. Bringing the client back online restored it within ~10s — the channel reconnected, re-helloed, and the forfeit was cancelled — while the client that stayed connected throughout was never swept. Zero page errors. *Why: the cheapest signal is the one someone else is already recording. Hibernation exists to avoid waking on keepalives, so any fix that inspects keepalives directly is self-defeating; asking the runtime when it last answered turns a per-ping cost into a per-half-minute one.* (2026-07-26) |

| D81 | A lobby seat's name is the ACCOUNT's, resolved server-side (P5 polish, increment P5-1) | The first P5 item, and the one a player notices before anything else: after twelve P4 increments the lobby still said "Player 6046". A seat's name was whatever the client announced in its `hello` — a handle generated into localStorage, editable by anyone, belonging to nobody. It is now the account's `displayName`, read at the hello by `loadDisplayName` from the same `userId` the /ws session cookie already resolved (the second use of the lobby's one authenticated fact, after the owner-scoped deck read). **Resolving rather than trusting is the decision**, and it is not only cosmetic: the moment names stop being random, a client-supplied name is an impersonation vector — announce yourself as your opponent's handle and the versus screen agrees. The read sits deliberately AFTER the refusal branches, so a socket that gets no seat costs no D1 query however often it retries, and hellos are rare in steady state (heartbeats keep the client's idle timer fresh, so it only re-announces after a real gap). **The fallback rule is the careful part:** a blank account name yields `null`, and the caller drops back to the client's announced handle — never to the EMAIL, which is the one substitution that suggests itself because `AccountButton` uses exactly that. That control shows a user their OWN address; a lobby name is broadcast to the opponent and, since 3c-vii, to spectators. A cosmetic blank is a smaller problem than a published email address, and a test pins it. The client announces its account name as well, which changes nothing authoritative — it only spares the host the half-second where their own seat reads "Player 4271" before the first broadcast corrects it, since the waiting screen is seeded locally. No server-side length cap: registration bounds names at 64, `PlayerPanel` already truncates, and mangling someone's name to fit a panel is the UI's job, not the wire's. 1878 → **1881** tests, `bun run check` green. **BROWSER-VERIFIED on four clients:** two signed-in seats read "Ash" and "Misty" across the player panels, the turn banner, the game log ("Ash wins the toss") and the spectator pill ("Watching — Ash vs Misty"), while two SIGNED-OUT players kept their generated handles with the lobby working normally. Zero page errors. *Why: a name is identity, and identity that the client asserts is not identity at all. The server already knew who the socket was — using that costs one query and closes an impersonation hole that only existed because nobody's name meant anything yet.* (2026-07-26) |

| D82 | Generated avatars from a hashed account id, not uploads (P5 polish, increment P5-2) | The other half of "lobby identity", and split from the uploads polish.md describes on purpose: an upload flow means R2, a CSP change, moderation questions and a settings surface, while what the lobby actually lacked was any face at all — `PlayerPanel` drew the same grey figure for everyone. **A generated avatar buys most of the value for none of that infrastructure:** `PlayerState.avatarSeed` carries a token the server derives at the hello from the account behind the socket, and `PlayerAvatar` draws a deterministic two-hue gradient with the account's initial. Nothing is stored, nothing is uploaded, and the property that matters holds — the same person looks the same to you in every lobby, which is what makes it identity rather than decoration (browser-verified across two clients: both saw identical gradients for the same accounts, in opposite seats). **It is a HASH of the account id, never the id.** Not because a uuid is guessable, but because the lobby snapshot is BROADCAST — to the opponent, and since 3c-vii to spectators — and an internal primary key is the wrong thing to publish there: it invites joining this seat to any other surface exposing the same id. FNV-1a is enough because this is a display token, not a security boundary; the client's only use is picking colours. **An anonymous seat gets NO seed and keeps the generic figure**, deliberately: the only id available for one is the per-lobby playerId, and a face derived from that would change on the player's next visit — promising an identity that isn't there is worse than admitting there is none. **Saturation and lightness are fixed**, so the seed picks the hue and never how loud the result is; that is what stops one player's face glowing next to another's in a UI built on restrained glass. An empty name draws a bare gradient rather than a placeholder letter, since a wrong initial is a claim and a gradient is not. The wire field cost one line in `readSnapshot`'s `withSeatDefaults` — the normalizer 3c-v added for exactly this, so a lobby persisted by the previous deploy survives the new field instead of being evicted. 1881 → **1889** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED on four clients:** two signed-in seats drew stable, visually distinct faces ("A" orange→amber, "M" cyan→indigo) with byte-identical gradients on both clients, and two signed-out seats kept the generic figure. A screenshot confirmed they sit in-palette against both the blue and red seat washes. *Why: the expensive half of avatars is storage and moderation; the valuable half is that people become recognisable. Deriving a face from the account you already authenticated delivers the second without buying the first, and leaves the upload path a strict improvement rather than a rewrite.* (2026-07-26) |

| D83 | A deck's cover is its highest-HP Pokémon, derived on read (P5 polish, increment P5-3) | The decks grid drew the same blue card back for every deck under a generated tint, while the catalog has had real scans since P2. **The slice's whole content is the RULE**, so it lives in a pure `pickCoverCardId` that can be argued with and tested rather than inside SQL: **the Pokémon with the highest printed HP**, ties broken by copies, then by card id for determinism. HP is the best proxy the catalog offers for "the card this deck is built around", and crucially it is one number rather than a taxonomy to interpret — an ex/V/VMAX or a Stage 2 outranks the Basics that fetch it WITHOUT anyone having to rank `stage` values against each other. The two obvious alternatives both fail on a real deck: ranking by STAGE gets a Basic-ex deck wrong (a 330 HP Basic ex is the payoff and would lose to any Stage 2 tech line), and ranking by COUNT gets nearly every evolution deck wrong (the 4-of Basic beats the 3-of Stage 2 it evolves into — verified live: Skeledirge ×3 correctly beat Fuecoco ×4). Cards with no scan are skipped rather than picked and rendered blank, and a deck with no qualifying card gets `coverCardId: null`, keeping the card back — which is also exactly right for a deck you have only just created (`fromDeck`, the create-response mapper, hardcodes null for that reason). **Derived on READ**, in one extra query for the whole library beside the existing `cardCount` aggregate: no stored column, so a cover follows the deck's contents with nothing to keep in sync, and no write path to change. It is a HEURISTIC and will occasionally pick a wall over the attacker beside it; the proper answer is letting the owner choose, which this leaves room for (a stored choice would simply win over it). **A browser run caught what tests could not:** the deck NAME, white text that had always sat on a flat blue back, was nearly illegible over flames and holo foil — so the label gained a gradient scrim, applied ONLY when there is art, so a coverless deck looks exactly as it did. 1889 → **1899** tests. *Why: the cheapest correct default beats a configuration surface nobody has asked for yet, and HP is the rare heuristic that is both trivially cheap and right on the decks that matter.* (2026-07-26) |

| D84 | The playmat's pass + history controls are DELETED, not relocated (P5 polish, increment P5-4) | The oldest open defect in the repo — "the Pass turn button is unclickable while the turn panel is open", carried since 2026-07-26 with a residual about the history arrows — closed by reading the code rather than the symptom. **Two findings changed the slice entirely.** First, `PreviousButton` and `ForwardButton` **took no props at all**: no `onClick`, no handler, on any surface, ever. They were chrome from the /simulator visual prototype, so the residual ("history navigation stays unreachable during your own turn:action") described navigation that DOES NOT EXIST — and three sessions of docs, mine included, had been treating them as blocked functionality. Two buttons a screen reader announces as "Previous"/"Forward" that do nothing are worse than no buttons: they promise a feature. They are gone, to return WIRED if a real history is ever built. Second, the ⟶ pass control is enabled **exactly when the turn panel renders over it** — the panel appears precisely when `passDisabled === false` — so on /play and online it was never clickable, and relocating it would have been moving a control whose replacement (each panel's own `Pass`) already exists and is browser-verified. **The API expresses the rule instead of a flag:** `PlaymatView.onPassTurn` became OPTIONAL, and the control renders only for a driver that passes one — "give the board a pass control by giving it something to call". The /simulator sandbox passes one (nothing covers it there); /play and online do not, and shed their now-dead `passTurn`/`passDisabled` wiring with it. Rejected: moving the controls to the left edge (the game log already owns bottom-left, and moving DEAD arrows would make them more prominent), and capping the panel's height (a real cost — a long attack/ability list gains a scrollbar — paid to keep a button nobody can use). **Browser-verified at 1280×700 with a real `elementFromPoint` hit-test**, because a synthetic `.click()` is precisely what disguised this bug for weeks: at a live turn:action, /play has no "Pass turn" and no arrows, its in-panel `Pass` hit-tests to itself and advances the turn (TURN 01 → 02); /simulator still has its ⟶, hit-testing to itself. The `verify` skill's entry — which had already been corrected once, from "an agent-browser quirk" to "a real product bug" — is now corrected again to describe the current controls and, more usefully, to state the general rule: eval may DRIVE, but only a hit-test may conclude a control works. 1899 tests, unchanged in count (one test switched from clicking the unreachable ⟶ to the panel's `Pass`). *Why: the fix for a control that cannot be reached is not a better position for it. Once one of the two was never wired and the other was permanently redundant, the honest change was subtraction — and the API that falls out ("pass a handler, get a button") is simpler than the one that was there.* (2026-07-26) |

| D85 | Your account is editable on /settings, and the avatar seed rides on `User` (P5 polish, increment P5-5) | P5-1 made a lobby seat's name the ACCOUNT's `displayName`, resolved server-side and broadcast to the opponent and to spectators — and left a player wearing whatever register picked, with nowhere to change it. **`PATCH /auth/me` + a Profile section on /settings** closes that: one required field (`updateProfileRequestSchema`, trim + 1–64, the same bounds register uses on its OPTIONAL name), `requireUser` BEFORE the validator so a signed-out caller hears "unauthorized" rather than a critique of their body, and no write at all when the name is unchanged. **The interesting decision is the FACE.** A profile that showed a name but no avatar would be a text box calling itself a profile, and one drawing a lookalike avatar would be worse — it would promise a face that isn't the one opponents see. So `userSchema` gained **`avatarSeed`**, derived by the same `avatarSeedFrom` D82 introduced, and the section renders the SAME `PlayerAvatar` the lobby does. That moved two things deliberately: the module to `apps/api/src/auth/avatar.ts` (the seed is a property of the ACCOUNT, not of a seat — lobby already imports from auth, not the reverse) and the component to `src/components/` (shared, so /settings and the lobby cannot drift into two similar drawings). A test pins `avatarSeedOf` against `avatarSeedFrom` for the same reason. **Deriving the seed client-side was rejected**: a second copy of FNV-1a in the web bundle is a hash that must agree with the server forever, and the day it doesn't a player's own face silently stops matching the one everyone else sees. Publishing it costs nothing — the lobby already broadcasts it. Smaller calls: the avatar's initial follows the DRAFT as you type, so the face and the field can never disagree on screen; a 401 on save re-probes the session so the panel becomes the sign-in prompt, which says it better than an error line under a dead form; the form is keyed by `user.id` so switching accounts re-seeds the field. A rename reaches a lobby at the next hello (`loadDisplayName` resolves the seat name there), so a player already seated elsewhere keeps the old name until they rejoin. 1899 → **1911** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED on two clients:** renaming "Brock" → "Pewter Brock" flipped the initial to "P" live, kept the gradient byte-identical (the seed is the account id, not the name), updated the corner account control with no reload, survived a reload, and — the point of the slice — **the opponent's client showed "Pewter Brock" with that same gradient**. Save and the field both hit-tested to themselves; the signed-out panel offers a sign-in link whose `state.from` returns to /settings. Zero page errors. *Why: an identity you cannot change isn't yours. And once the profile's job is "how you appear to other players", showing anything other than the exact artifacts the lobby broadcasts would make the page a mock-up of itself.* (2026-07-26) |

| D86 | A deck cover is a PIN over the derived default, resolved on read (P5 polish, increment P5-6) | P5-3 fronted every deck with its highest-HP Pokémon and said outright that the proper answer was letting the owner choose. This is that: a nullable `decks.cover_card_id` the editor sets, and a pure **`effectiveCoverCardId(chosen, candidates)`** the list query runs — **the pin wins, and everything else falls through to `pickCoverCardId`**. The derived rule is untouched; it is now explicitly the DEFAULT rather than the answer. **Three decisions carry the slice.** First, **the resolution runs against the candidate list the default was already deriving from**, so honouring a choice costs NO extra query, and a pin that has gone stale (its card removed elsewhere, or its scan gone after a re-ingest) silently falls back instead of drawing a blank rectangle — a deck must never front a card it doesn't run. Second, **the pin may be a TRAINER or an Energy while the derived default stays Pokémon-only**: guessing needs a rule, choosing does not, and a signature Supporter is a legitimate face (browser-verified with Academy at Night, which the rule could never pick). Third, **two fields, deliberately not one**: `DeckSummary.coverCardId` remains the face being DRAWN (so the grid needed no change at all), while the full `Deck` carries `chosenCoverCardId`, the stored CHOICE the editor's picker is set to — null for almost every deck. Collapsing them into one name would have made "what is drawn" and "what was chosen" the same word for two different questions. **`Automatic` is an explicit option in the picker**, not the absence of one, so reverting is one click; it deliberately shows no art, because the default is a RULE and drawing today's answer to it would read as "this card". **The consistency rule lives on both sides:** PATCH validates the pin against the card list the patch LEAVES BEHIND (400 `cover card not in deck`) and drops a pin whose card that patch removes, while the editor's `toSnapshot` drops it locally too — not cosmetic, since the cover rides the same debounced PATCH as the card list, and a self-contradicting body would 400 forever (the saver retries the same dirty snapshot). The cover joining that one save path is what keeps the pair atomic. 1911 → **1932** tests; migration `0004`. **BROWSER-VERIFIED end to end at 1920×1080:** pinning the Trainer put it on the library tile, removing it dropped the pin, kept saving ("Saved", PATCH 200 — the wedge that would have followed a naive implementation) and fell back to Absol; a pin survived a reload through GET /decks/:id; a hand-crafted PATCH naming a card outside the deck got the 400; and both the footer control and a picker tile hit-tested to themselves. *Why: a heuristic that is right most of the time plus an override that is always right beats trying to make the heuristic cleverer — and the override is only trustworthy if the two can never disagree about what the deck contains.* (2026-07-26) |

## Locked assumptions (override explicitly if they change)

  our Zod schemas** — the official `@tcgdex/sdk` turned out unnecessary since
  we validate every payload ourselves anyway (changed 2026-07-09, was: SDK).

  improved iteratively.

## These are defaults, not law
Every decision and assumption here is a **default with a rationale**, chosen with
the context available at the time — revisit any of them when the code or new
context reveals a better path. The point of writing them down is to preserve the
*why*, so a later session can judge whether it still holds.

## Adding / changing a decision
Append a row (or a dated subsection for bigger ones) with the choice **and the
one-line why**. When you revise an existing decision, update its row and note
what changed and why. The one hard rule: **don't reverse a decision silently** —
leave a trail so the reasoning is never lost.

# Workstream: Polish (Phase 5)

Refinements unlocked once real **user** and **card** data exist. Threads through
P2–P4; tracked here so nothing is forgotten.

## Backlog
- **PASS / HISTORY CONTROLS — CLOSED 2026-07-26 (P5-4, D84).** The long-running
  "the Pass turn button is unclickable while the turn panel is open" item, and
  its residual about the history arrows, are both resolved — by DELETION, once
  the code was read rather than the symptom described:
  - **`PreviousButton`/`ForwardButton` took no props.** No `onClick`, no handler,
    on any surface, ever. They were mock chrome from the /simulator prototype, so
    "history navigation is unreachable during your own turn:action" described
    navigation that did not exist. Two buttons a screen reader announced as
    "Previous"/"Forward" and that did nothing are worse than none; they are gone.
    If a real history is built, they come back WIRED.
  - **The playmat's ⟶ was enabled exactly when the panel covered it** — the panel
    renders precisely when `passDisabled === false` — so on /play and online it
    was never clickable. `PlaymatView.onPassTurn` is now OPTIONAL and the control
    renders only for a driver that passes one: the /simulator sandbox, where
    nothing covers it. Each game panel has carried its own `Pass` since the
    earlier fix, browser-verified.
  Verified in a browser at 1280×700 with a real `elementFromPoint` hit-test (a
  synthetic `.click()` is what hid the original bug): at a live turn:action /play
  has no "Pass turn" and no arrows, its in-panel `Pass` hit-tests to itself and
  advances the turn; /simulator still has its ⟶, hit-testing to itself.
- **Lobby identity — NAMES DONE 2026-07-26 (P5-1, D81); avatars still open.** A
  lobby seat's name is now the ACCOUNT's `displayName`, resolved SERVER-SIDE at
  the hello (`loadDisplayName`, apps/api/src/lobby/displayName.ts) from the same
  `userId` the /ws session cookie already provided — so it is authoritative, not
  announced, and a player cannot present themselves as someone else. An anonymous
  socket (or an account whose name is blank) keeps the client's generated
  "Player 4271" handle; the blank case deliberately does NOT fall back to the
  email, which `AccountButton` shows a user about themselves but which a lobby
  broadcasts to the opponent AND to spectators. The client announces its account
  name too, purely so the host's locally-seeded waiting screen doesn't flash the
  old handle. Browser-verified: signed-in seats read "Ash"/"Misty" across panels,
  turn banner, game log and the spectator pill, while two signed-out players kept
  their generated handles. **AVATARS (generated) DONE 2026-07-26 (P5-2, D82):**
  `PlayerState.avatarSeed` carries an FNV-1a HASH of the account id (never the id
  — the snapshot is broadcast to the opponent and to spectators), from which
  `PlayerAvatar` draws a deterministic two-hue gradient plus the same initial the
  account control shows. Nothing stored, nothing uploaded, and the same person
  looks the same to you in every lobby; an anonymous seat keeps the generic
  figure rather than being given a face that would change next visit. Saturation
  and lightness are FIXED so the seed picks the hue and never how loud the result
  is. **Still open: uploaded avatars** — the item below (R2 + CSP); an image
  simply wins over the generated one when it lands.
- **Profiles — NAME + FACE DONE 2026-07-26 (P5-5, D85); favourite deck open.**
  The Profile section on **/settings** (`src/features/settings/
  ProfileSection.tsx`) is where an account edits itself, and the first thing it
  fixes is that P5-1 made your name authoritative and broadcast while leaving it
  unchangeable. **`PATCH /auth/me`** (requireUser BEFORE the validator; no write
  when nothing changed) takes `updateProfileRequestSchema` — one required
  `displayName`, trimmed, 1–64, the same bounds register applies to its optional
  one. The provider's `updateProfile` adopts the api's answer as the current
  user, so the corner account control follows with no re-probe.
  **The section shows the REAL generated avatar, not a lookalike:** `userSchema`
  now carries **`avatarSeed`** (derived server-side, the same value the lobby
  broadcasts), so `PlayerAvatar` — moved to `src/components/` since two surfaces
  use it — draws the identical face here and in a lobby. The seed module moved
  with it, to `apps/api/src/auth/avatar.ts`: it is a property of the ACCOUNT, not
  of a seat. Deriving the hash client-side was rejected — a second copy of FNV-1a
  is one that must agree with the server forever.
  The initial follows the draft as you type; a 401 mid-save re-probes and the
  panel becomes a sign-in prompt (`state.from` returns you here). **A rename
  reaches a lobby at the next hello** (`loadDisplayName` resolves the seat name
  there), so a player already seated keeps the old name until they rejoin.
  Browser-verified across two clients: "Brock" → "Pewter Brock" updated the
  initial, the corner control and the OPPONENT's player panel, with a
  byte-identical gradient throughout (the seed is the id, not the name).
  **Still open: a favourite deck** on the profile, and the uploads below.
- **Avatars:** upload/choose an avatar → stored in R2, served from our domain;
  update CSP accordingly. The settings surface P5-2 said this needed now exists
  (the Profile section above), so what's left is genuinely the R2 + CSP +
  moderation half; an uploaded image simply wins over the generated face.
- **Deck covers / art — DONE 2026-07-26 (P5-3, D83).** A deck is fronted by its
  own headline card. **The rule (pure `pickCoverCardId`, apps/api/src/decks/
  cover.ts): the Pokémon with the highest printed HP**, ties broken by copies
  then card id. HP is the best proxy the catalog offers for "the card this deck
  is built around" and needs no taxonomy: ranking by STAGE gets a Basic-ex deck
  wrong, ranking by COUNT gets nearly every evolution deck wrong (the 4-of Basic
  beats the 3-of Stage 2 it evolves into). Cards with no scan are skipped;
  `coverCardId` is null for an empty or Pokémon-less deck and the blue back
  stands, which is also right for a deck you just created. Derived on READ in the
  list query (one extra query for the whole library, no stored column to keep in
  sync). It is a HEURISTIC — a user-chosen cover would simply win over it, and
  that's the natural follow-up. **A browser run caught the thing tests couldn't:**
  the deck name was nearly illegible over busy card art (it had always sat on a
  flat blue back), so the label now gets a gradient scrim — only when there IS
  art, so a coverless deck looks exactly as before.
  **A CHOSEN cover — DONE 2026-07-26 (P5-6, D86).** The follow-up above, built:
  a nullable `decks.cover_card_id` (migration `0004`) the editor pins, and a pure
  **`effectiveCoverCardId(chosen, candidates)`** (apps/api/src/decks/cover.ts) the
  list query runs — the pin wins, everything else falls through to
  `pickCoverCardId`, which is now explicitly the DEFAULT rather than the answer.
  It resolves against the candidate list the default was already deriving from,
  so a choice costs no extra query and a STALE pin (card removed elsewhere, scan
  gone after a re-ingest) falls back rather than drawing a blank. The pin may be
  a **Trainer** — guessing needs a rule, choosing does not. Two fields on purpose:
  `DeckSummary.coverCardId` is still the face being DRAWN (the grid needed no
  change), while `Deck.chosenCoverCardId` is the stored CHOICE the picker is set
  to. The picker (`CoverDialog`, opened from the deck panel's footer) offers
  **Automatic as an explicit option** — reverting is one click — and only cards
  the catalog can draw. **Consistency is enforced on both sides:** PATCH validates
  the pin against the list the patch leaves behind (400 `cover card not in deck`)
  and drops a pin whose card it removes; the editor's `toSnapshot` drops it
  locally too, which is load-bearing — the cover rides the same debounced PATCH
  as the card list, so a self-contradicting body would 400 forever.
- **Card detail view:** richer card view using tcgdex fields (attacks, abilities,
  pricing, set/illustrator).
- **Settings & accessibility:** carry the existing `prefers-reduced-motion`
  respect through the new surfaces.

Pull items into an active phase as they become relevant; don't build them ahead
of the data they need.
